title: The Robot I Didn’t Expect to Build
gist: Agility Robotics co-founder Jonathan Hurst explains how customer, safety and regulatory demands turned Digit 5 into a 120+ kg, forklift-like warehouse humanoid (23-kg bin lifts, 90-minute runtime, 9-minute charge, 10,000+ units/year factory capacity) far from his original graceful vision. He argues the trade-offs are necessary for any humanoid to do real work safely today.

insights.claim: Agility Robotics launched Digit 5, a humanoid weighing over 120 kg that lifts 23-kg bins onto 1.75-meter shelves, matching NIOSH lifting guidelines for human workers.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Sets the capability bar a warehouse humanoid must clear to be commercially credible.

insights.claim: Digit 5 runs 90 minutes per charge and fully recharges in a 9-minute break at a dock delivering 240 amperes at 48 volts, enabling near-continuous 20-hour-a-day work that no human can do.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Fast-charge docking, not battery size alone, drives the labor-replacement economics; watch uptime claims in deployments.

insights.claim: The battery and cooling system occupy about 75 percent of Digit 5's torso, and the robot can no longer run or jump like earlier generations.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Power and thermal packaging is the binding constraint on humanoid form factor.
insights.quote: The battery and cooling system takes up about 75 percent of Digit’s torso

insights.claim: Agility's RoboFab in Salem, Oregon is a 70,000-square-foot facility with capacity to produce more than 10,000 Digit 5 robots per year.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Stated capacity, not output; compare against actual unit shipments as a test of the scaling claim.

insights.claim: Hurst calls Digit 5 the scaling moment for Agility, the inflection point for deploying robots in large numbers, and describes it as the largest, heaviest and most expensive robot Agility will ever build.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Management frames this generation as a cost-heavy but volume-enabling product; check pricing and order backlog.
insights.quote: I believe Digit 5 will be the scaling moment for Agility Robotics

insights.claim: In Digit 4 commercial deployments, robots had to work behind physical barriers, separated from humans, to meet insurance and regulatory demands, which severely limited their usefulness.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Insurance and regulation, not only technology, gate humanoid deployment next to workers.

insights.claim: Agility spent two years making Digit 5 able to operate safely beside people, and it shaped the legs, body, safety-rated sensors in protective housings, and isolated safety computers.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Certifiable safety adds large engineering cost and time; competitors without it face the same wall.
insights.quote: We spent two years on this challenge.

insights.claim: When a person approaches, Digit 5 is programmed to stop, set down its payload, sit on the floor and cut motor power before the person can touch it, a conservative verifiable approach Agility considers the only sensible first step.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Verifiable stop-and-sit behavior is the compliance template to watch for in rival humanoid safety cases.
insights.locator: Digit 5 is designed to be the first humanoid robot that can operate safely

insights.claim: Safety features raise Digit 5's complexity, power consumption, mass and physical size, which Hurst concedes feels like a massive slowdown on the path toward robots in everyday life.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Safety requirements push humanoids toward industrial, caged-free niches before consumer use.

insights.claim: Digit 5 must meet European CE compliance, North American UL electrical-safety certification and FCC electromagnetic radiation limits, which Hurst calls absolute requirements.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Certification burden is a barrier to entry that favors well-funded, customer-driven humanoid makers.
insights.locator: These realities include things like European CE

themes.theme: Function over form in humanoid design

insights.claim: Digit 5 replaced the ostrichlike backward legs with humanlike legs because the ankle struck the ground when squatting, and knee and hip motors now both contribute torque to stand up under load.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Heavy near-floor lifting pushed even a bipedal pioneer toward the standard humanoid leg layout.
insights.locator: The most visible change with Digit 5

insights.claim: Hurst argues that a humanoid seen working in a factory or warehouse either can't lift the required weight or can't last a whole shift, and if it is not covered with sensors it is likely not safe to stand next to.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: A skeptical lens for evaluating rival humanoid demo videos against real shift-length payload and safety specs.
insights.quote: If you see a robot that looks like a human working in a factory or warehouse, it either can’t lift the required weight or can’t make it through the whole shift.

insights.claim: Hurst says other humanoid makers have copied the human form without understanding its purpose, and that without matching function the point of the human form may be lost.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Form-first humanoid companies may carry design risk versus function-driven ones.
insights.quote: Making a robot look like a human is the easy part

insights.claim: Hurst says Digit 5 feels more like a forklift than the graceful humanoid he set out to build, and he admits he cannot love it.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: The founder's candor signals how far commercial humanoids sit from the research vision.
insights.quote: In some ways, Digit 5 feels more like a forklift than the graceful humanoid I set out to build.

themes.theme: From research lab to commercial product

insights.claim: Agility sold only 10 Cassie bipedal research robots at US $250,000 each to universities including Harvard, Caltech, Michigan and Berkeley, saturating that research market.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: The research-robot market was too small to sustain a company, forcing the move to commercial work.
insights.locator: Cassie was the first dynamic bipedal robot

insights.claim: Cassie enabled researchers to pioneer reinforcement learning for bipedal locomotion, where a simulated robot learns by trial and error and the resulting neural network controls the physical machine, underlying virtually all dynamic legged-robot behavior today.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Sim-to-real reinforcement learning is the foundation of current legged robot control, a key AI-robotics capability.

insights.claim: Hurst says the founders did not start from a customer problem; they trusted themselves to figure out the business as they went, and found the answer in moving bins in warehouses.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Illustrates technology-push humanoid startups needing a constrained first job to find product-market fit.
insights.quote: My cofounders, Damion Shelton and Mikhail Jones, and I did not do this.
insights.locator: Good advice for starting a company

insights.claim: Bin handling suited Digit because two arms are needed to lift large bins high, legs balance in narrow spaces, and the task varies too much across sites for single-purpose automation.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Defines the niche where humanoids beat fixed automation: variable, constrained, human-scaled tasks.
insights.locator: As we explored the first applications for Digit

insights.claim: Digit's pilot history includes Ford carrying packages from an autonomous vehicle to a porch, a package-delivery company sorting boxes, Amazon testing Digit 4, and Digit 4 becoming the world's first commercially deployed humanoid at logistics provider GXO.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Names the logistics customers validating humanoid pilots; GXO is the commercial reference deployment.

insights.claim: Keeping early deployments operational consumed huge effort and arguably eliminated Agility's profit, even though it kept the company learning.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Early humanoid deployments carry heavy service costs, so margins depend on reliability gains.
insights.quote: We spent a huge amount of time and effort keeping our first deployments operational, which arguably eliminated any profit we made.

insights.claim: Agility recruited a new executive team that pushed Digit 4 EVT from a minor upgrade to major changes in a compressed timeline, adding larger batteries and safety and regulatory upgrades that added mass and changed its appearance.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Professional management shifted priorities from the founder's vision toward productization.
insights.locator: We had intended the next revision of Digit

insights.claim: After mapping the first 10 use cases from Digit 4 EVT deployments, Agility designed Digit 5 from scratch around customer realities.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Deployment-led design means the roadmap follows customer tasks.
insights.locator: Digit 5 will be Agility’s first real step

insights.claim: Agility's road map extends beyond carrying bins to picking individual items, tending machines, preparing parts for assembly and shipping, and eventually assembly work, using interchangeable tool interfaces and modular upgradable subsystems.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Expansion into machine tending and assembly widens the addressable market; track which tasks ship first.

insights.claim: Hurst expects Digit 5 to serve as a platform for improvement and a source of data for future behavior training, while also being a viable product.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Fleet data as a training asset ties deployment scale to future AI capability gains.

insights.claim: Hurst says customer and product requirements did not ruin his vision but revealed what it was missing, and that future Digits should be lighter and more graceful.
insights.speaker: Jonathan W. Hurst
insights.so_what: Signals a later generation could regain agility once the commercial base exists.
insights.quote: Customers and product requirements didn’t ruin my vision; they revealed what my vision was missing.
